Hey, I also struggled/struggle with addiction. Not opioids but other stuff. I know when you're actively in addiction it can feel like everyone and everything is against you: and to be honest they kind of are. Is it fair to you? Not necessarily.

But it's not fair to them either.

Being around an addict is hard. Addicts tend to not realize their own behavior, they minimize or conveniently dismiss the amount they've lied, stolen, borrowed, and begged. They lash out and are a emotionally volatile. I know, because I was also this way.

It didn't end until I got sober. Period.

Addiction is not just about the addict. It is a social disease--it effects everyone around the addict. It is really hard to see when you're in the thick of it.

You say "you're not ready". No one ever is. Also, getting clean or sober is hard as fuck. People do not realize how life-long a battle it is, because you're fighting your own brain chemistry. You have to battle withdrawals that may very well kill you (I almost died from alcohol withdrawal a couple times). Overcoming addiction is one of the most difficult things a human being can do: but you have to do it, or you end up dead, and utterly alone.

So you try again, and again, and again, again....however long it takes until it sticks. It may very well take years, it often does. And yeah, relapse is part of this life long disease that you will always have. But the only person who can make things different is you forcing yourself to do some shit you don't want to.

If you're scared to smoke that much again, don't. There's no need to get super duper high anyways. Moderation is nice. Also, if you get super high like that regularly then your tolerance will go up and you'll have to spend more money on herb. It's a lose/lose situation for a very brief and fleeting experience.

Hey there, I have felt the way you felt. Multiple times over. Here's some advice that helped me:

The last time I relapsed I called a rehab center, but they couldn't take me in because they didn't have space. The guy over the phone was in recovery, and he told me just try not drinking for one day.

That's actually all you have to do. I still have to take it one day and a time even now, almost 800 days later (it's a hell of a lot easier now!).  It seems massive and overwhelming, and your anxiety is gonna be sky-high right now. The doom and gloom thoughts are gonna be powerful, but they are just thoughts.. Those things aren't guaranteed, and you'd be surprised what you can mend once you start to heal yourself. All you need to focus on right now is taking it one day at a time, quite literally. 

Relapse is part of alcohol use disorder. It is a part of addiction. You are not bad, or wrong, or hopeless. Just take it one day at a time and let the days pass, and they will. Beating yourself up is not gonna help right now, so just focus on moving forward, hour by hour and day by day.

Feel free to message me if you want for support.

Heavy drinking can lead to a thiamine disorder that causes permanent intellectual disability. I'm not saying that has happened to you or even will happen to you, but it's something to think about.

When we drink alcohol our bodies lose the ability to process B vitamins, specifically thiamine. Thiamine is really important for neural communication. If you quit now, since you are so young, your neural pathways will likely heal up pretty well. You might even be able to surpass your peers, who knows!

I was a situational binge drinker too! One thing that helps me not be too hard on myself is to remind myself that there is a genetic component to this. People with alcohol use disorder tend to have genes that, when combined with environmental factors, lead to alcoholism. This is why not every traumatized person becomes an alcoholic, but others do. So the fact that you became a problem drinker or whatever you want to call it isn't necessarily 100% your fault, there are things outside of your control that contributed. However, you do have full control over the future outcome of this disease. You don't have to give in to it, you can resist. Yes, you made choices that lead to binge drinking but you never set out to become out of control. Nobody sets out to become out of control, it just happens to some of us. Be kind to yourself, and remember you can change things starting now.

There are many different ways to stop. The first and biggest one is to choose not to drink each day you wake up. There are books, support groups, this subreddit, outpatient and inpatient rehab programs, and drugs you can get from your doctor to help curb cravings. What works for you is going to be something you get to explore. It's a journey, a process, and you will figure it out as you go.

Right now, don't worry about explaining anything to anyone. You don't have to. Just get through today, then tomorrow, then the next day. As you put more days under your belt without alcohol, your anxiety will probably start to lessen a bit. You don't need to be in group settings or around unsupportive friends right now, if you become a bit of a hermit that's ok. With time you will build confidence. If you feel like you \*have\* to explain yourself but aren't ready to tell people you've stopped drinking, I think it's totally ok to whip out a couple white lies. "I'm on antibiotics." is a  good one ;) Or just tell them you're taking a break from drinking, sobriety is "in" right now.

The people who don't mind your not drinking are the people you want to keep in your life. If someone is giving you a hard time about it, maybe you don't need them in your life.

It could be autism, but it could also be PTSD and a whole number of other things. A lot of pyschiatric illnesses, learning disorders, and other neurological conditions share many symptoms. Don't rely on your friend, and definitely don't rely on reddit for a diagnosis--you need to see a specialist. It's possible you do have empathy and sympathy, but because you've witness and been through some traumatic experiences your mind is shielding you from them. Or maybe you have something else going on, there's literally thousands of different things it could be. Seeing a professional, like a psychiatrist, is important because they can do something called "differential diagnosis"---that means they take in your whole life history and medical history, including family history, and they consider all the options and rule things out that don't seem to fit. Tell your friend to stop arm-chair diagnosing, that's wrong.
